title: What social teaching is
hookLine: a pope writes a letter about wages, strikes and the poor, and a new strand of teaching begins

lines: A PAYCHECK, A FACTORY, A LANDLORD.
cards: No incense today. No cloister. Today starts with a paycheck that runs out before the month does, a factory floor, a landlord at the door.
A pope, Leo the Thirteenth, wrote a long letter about exactly those things: workers and owners, wages and strikes, property and the poor.

It opens with two Latin words, rerum novarum, of new things, and they became its name. The new things were the changes in work and cities Leo saw around him. A new block of the path begins with that letter.

teach.h: A BODY OF TEACHING, NOT ONE BOOK.
teach.b: First, what the phrase names. Catholic social teaching isn't one book.

It's a body of teaching built up from popes' letters, councils and bishops, and gathered in the Catechism, about how a society should be ordered so people can flourish in it: wages, housing, war, migration, the earth itself.
Second, where it comes from. The Church says it isn't a new invention bolted onto the faith.

teach.h: GROWN FROM THE IMAGE OF GOD.
teach.b: It grows from the conviction that every person is made in God's image, and from Jesus' own words about feeding the hungry and welcoming the stranger. Third, the line that holds its spirit.

teach.h: NOT IN WORD, BUT IN DEED.
teach.b: The first letter of John says, in the Douay-Rheims: "My little children, let us not love in word, nor in tongue, but in deed, and in truth." Social teaching is that sentence, scaled up.

Helping the one neighbor at your door is charity, and the Church never stops asking for it. Asking why so many neighbors keep coming to the same door, and what could change that, is where social teaching begins.
That's love, organized. Fourth, what it isn't. John Paul the Second wrote that the Church doesn't offer technical solutions or a political program.
It offers principles, and leaves applying them to people in each place, who may disagree about how.
Catholics can land on different sides of a political argument and still be asked to measure their choices by the same principles.
Over the coming days, this block takes them one at a time: dignity, community, rights and duties, the poor, work, solidarity, creation.

how: Catholics meet social teaching in papal letters called encyclicals, in the Catechism, in homilies, and in parish and diocesan work for the poor, workers and migrants; some parishes run study groups on it.

o: the Church's teaching on justice in how society is built
the Church's rules for Catholics who hold public office
a parish program that runs food banks and shelters

games.q: you're a pope, and the questions on your desk are wages, strikes, property and the poor. what do you do?
o: leave it alone: the Church sticks to prayer.
write a letter on workers and owners, grounded in the faith.
draw up a detailed economic plan every country must adopt.
games.why: Leo XIII wrote Rerum Novarum. it gave principles, not a blueprint, and later popes said plainly that the Church offers no technical solutions.

practice: Take the line from John, not in word, but in deed, or one paragraph of Rerum Novarum if you have it, and let one question stay: where in my week does care stay at the level of words?
A cause talked about and never touched, perhaps, or a problem met one person at a time that might have a root. Don't solve it, just see it clearly; if you pray, bring it to God.

wordCard.voice: Catholic social teaching. The Church's body of teaching on justice in society, from Leo's letter on: love put to work in the way a society is built. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: of new things. the opening words of Leo XIII's letter, and so its name.

carryVoice: Your line: love, organized. Charity at the door, and a question about why the line keeps forming. See you tomorrow.
